rationale: B wins because its best angles are sharper at the actual reporting pressure point: "Bumble's AI writes the opening message on the app built around who sends it" is a cleaner, meaner story than A's fuzzier "Dating apps add AI to write your opening line - and some users hate it." A is careful and commercially useful, especially on proof, but B's questions like "whether the recipient can tell" find the story a reporter would actually chase. Dock B hard for inventing "first substantive product move," but the strategic material is still stronger.
gaps_in_A: "to fix the company she built" assigns motive. The facts support a return after decline and a relaunch, not the founder's inner purpose.
"Dating apps add AI to write your opening line" makes a plural category claim from one Bumble update. A admits this later, but the headline still gets ahead of the proof.
"Dorsey/Schultz/Kalanick-adjacent storyline" is clever-person shorthand, not useful reporter targeting. It decorates a solid founder-return angle instead of sharpening it.
A asks how AI interacts with women-message-first, but misses the nastier proof question: can the recipient tell the opener was AI-assisted? That could change the whole pitch posture.
gaps_in_B: "the first substantive product move since the founder's return this year" is invented. The update says the relaunch is under the returning founder-CEO, not that it is her first major move.
"AI writes the opening message" overstates "helps users write opening messages." The proof section backs off, but the headline is still too confident.
"the company has made a claim the next disclosure will settle" is too strong. The update gives a relaunch after decline, not a stated company claim or target.
The next step, "newsjack-detector," is a detour after a supplied company update. The useful move is current-coverage check plus journalist-fit-check on the strongest angle.
